result.summary: Mercury, having punished Aglauros, is sent by Jupiter to drive the king's herd toward the Sidonian shore where Europa plays. Jupiter turns himself into a gentle white bull, wins Europa's trust, and carries her out over the sea.

scenes.title: Jupiter sends Mercury to Sidon
scenes.summary: After punishing Aglauros, Mercury is called by his father and told to drive the king's cattle to the shore. The herd heads toward the beach where Europa plays.

scenes.title: The bull wins Europa
scenes.summary: Jupiter lays aside his majesty and becomes a gentle, snow-white bull among the herd. Europa overcomes her fear, feeds and garlands him, and sits on his back.
scenes.stakes: Europa risks her freedom and safety by trusting the disguised god.

scenes.title: Carried across the sea
scenes.summary: The bull wades into the waves and swims far out to sea. Europa looks back at the shore in fear, clutching his horn.
scenes.stakes: Europa is carried away from home over open sea, afraid.

alias_notes.explanation: Mercury's mother Maia was a daughter of Atlas.
Patronymic naming Europa through her father, king Agenor.

notable_quotes.reason: A memorable maxim that majesty and love cannot dwell together.
Vivid image of the bull's snow-white color.

analysis.text: Divine desire leads Jupiter to give up his dignity and use deception, a recurring pattern of gods' transformations and mortal vulnerability in the Metamorphoses.
The tale explains the origin of Europe's name and links Phoenicia with Crete, reflecting Greek myths of eastern origins for royal houses.

legacy.text: The abduction of Europa became a favorite subject in art, including Titian's painting The Rape of Europa (1560s) and Veronese's version.
A bull carrying a woman across the sea appears on the Greek 2-euro coin, which depicts Europa.

fun_facts.text: The Greek 2-euro coin shows Europa on the bull, based on a mosaic from Sparta.

language_notes.text: Grandson of Atlas is Mercury, whose mother Maia was Atlas's daughter. 'Lands named after Pallas' means Attica, the territory of Athens, whose goddess was Pallas Minerva.
Sidonis is the region around Sidon in Phoenicia. It looks toward Maia, Mercury's mother, because she is the Pleiad star; the note's 'Constellation' marks that.
'Three-forked flames' means Jupiter's thunderbolt, imagined with three prongs. 'Shakes the world with his nod' echoes a Homeric image of his power.
The horns seem so perfect that you might think they were handmade, polished like gems or horn carved by an artist.
Daughter of Agenor is Europa, princess of Tyre or Sidon; Agenor was the Phoenician king.
'Fictitious' means false or feigned: the hoofs belong to a disguise, not to a real bull.

context_notes.text: This heading summarizes the myth: Crete, where Jupiter takes Europa, becomes home to their son Minos. The continent Europe was later said to take her name.
Tyrian virgins are young women of Tyre, the Phoenician city. Europa's father's kingdom lay on this coast.

literary_notes.text: The narrator states a general truth, that grandeur and passion cannot coexist, to justify why Jupiter must give up his majesty.
Comparing the bull's color to untouched snow stresses his purity and harmlessness, hiding the god's real intent.
The repeated 'scarcely, oh, scarcely' is an emotional aside that exposes the god's desire beneath his gentle behavior.
The reader knows the bull is Jupiter, but Europa does not, which makes her trusting act ominous.
The clutched horn, the hand on his back and the ruffled garments give a vivid, fearful picture of her abduction.
